text: **Prompt Profiles** 是一个 DSH 网页端插件：为会话提供可复用的系统提示词配置。它注册提示词段落和配置档案，并在系统提示词组装时按档案顺序插入段落，支持主会话与子代理范围、模板变量、预览编辑及按工作区选择。适合需要在不同任务间切换写作规范或工作角色的 DSH 用户；选择结果会随会话封存。需要兼容指定 DSH 版本及其存储、工作区和网页界面服务，不需要 API 密钥。

**Prompt Profiles** adds reusable ordered prompt sections grouped into per-workspace profiles for DSH web sessions. Sections support scope and template variables; the settings editor previews them, and each session keeps its chosen composition. Requires compatible DSH services; no API key.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 📦 @knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles：> **This repository is archived.** Read-only: no further releases, no issue triage. The plugin still works on the DSH release it targets, but the problem it solves is now covered by the platform itself. Read [why](#why-it-is-archived) and [how to get the same result without it](#migrating-from-prompt-profiles-to-an-agent-preset). The reference documentation below stays for anyone still running an installed copy.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Why it is archived：**The platform grew the same axis.** This bundle added a "how the agent is told to work" dimension next to agent presets. Agent presets have since become the first-party home for exactly that: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset` declares an agent's child rows as ordinary YAML, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-persona` owns the persona prefix and suffix slots inside a preset. One preset per voice does what one profile did, and it does it through the platform's own loader, prompt registry, and documentation instead of a second implementation of each.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Why it is archived：**What that buys over this plugin.** The bundle has to shadow the assembled prompt, keep sealed per-session snapshots under `$DSH_HOME/storages/prompt_profiles/`, and write its own definition rows into `cordis.patch.yml`. It also pins a peer window (`>=0.1.7-rc.2 <0.2.2-0`) and needs `dsh plugin allow-version` outside it, and it injects two client packages to draw the composer chip and the editor. A preset composition declares the package it mounts and nothing else: no version exemption, no storage to reap, no client injection, and the persona text sits in the same YAML block as the tools and permissions it goes with, so "what the agent is" and "how it is told to work" are read and reviewed in one place.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Why it is archived：**It found no users.** The npm registry reports zero downloads for the package, and the only installation I know of is mine. A bundle nobody installs costs a re-verification pass on every DSH release window and returns nothing. Archiving is the honest outcome; a fork is one `git clone` away if you disagree.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Migrating from prompt profiles to an agent preset：The mapping is nearly mechanical: one profile becomes one preset, its sections become that preset's persona `prefix` (or its `suffix`, for text that belonged after the first-party guidance rather than before it), and the preset is picked when a session starts instead of in the composer chip.
section: Migrating from prompt profiles to an agent preset

text: @knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 1. Inventory what you actually have：Profiles and sections live as rows in your profile composition (`cordis.patch.yml` for a web profile, `~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml` for a shared install), under the `prompt-profiles` insert row. Read them out before deleting anything, or open **Settings → Prompt profiles → Preview**, which shows each profile in position among the built-in sections — that ordering is what the preset has to reproduce.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 2. Declare one preset per profile：Start from your baseline preset (usually `standard`) and add a persona row. The `persona` row must be mounted inside a preset: mounted globally it collides with the prompt registry's own persona registration and fails loud. The collision is the design, not an accident — the row exists to shadow the deployment persona for one agent.

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: preset-reviewer
      name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset'
      config:

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 2. Declare one preset per profile：`prefix` is required and `suffix` defaults to empty, so an omitted suffix does not inherit the global one. Both are templates: `{{…}}` groups resolve strictly against registered prompt variables at render time, the same strictness the sealer applied here. Two further fields matter. `complete: true` keeps only the prefix as the system prompt, which is how a `minimal`-style preset already works. `includeRuntimeContext: false` drops optional runtime context for that agent.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 3. Reproduce what `scope` was doing：This is the one place the mapping is not mechanical. A prompt-profiles section could be `inherit`, `main-only`, or `subagents-only`; a preset has no per-section scope, it has one composition. Text that only ever addressed subagents belongs in a preset those subagents are created with, not in the parent's persona — whether that is convenient depends on how you spawn them. If neither split suits you, folding the text into the parent persona is the pragmatic answer, and a subagent simply reads guidance it does not act on.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 4. Choose the preset instead of the profile：Presets are selected per session in the platform UI before the session starts, and the registry's `default` and `selectedDefault` decide what a new session gets without a choice. The equivalent of picking `None` is the `standard` preset: both mean "the session runs with the platform's own prompt". Sessions already running keep the composition they were created with, exactly as they kept the profile they were sealed with.
section: 4. Choose the preset instead of the profile

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · 5. Remove the plugin and its leftovers：```bash
dsh plugin --profile web remove @knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles
```

Then restart DSH, delete the `prompt-profiles` insert row from the composition (the definitions the writer stored there go with it), and delete `$DSH_HOME/storages/prompt_profiles/` so the sealed snapshots do not linger.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · What the migration loses：- The editor: profile and section lists, drag-and-drop ordering, in-place preview among built-in sections, search, debounced autosave, three UI languages.
- Reuse: a section referenced by five profiles was one string with five placements. A preset inlines its own text; share it with a YAML anchor or duplicate it.
- The composer chip and its per-workspace memory, including the explicit `None` decision.
- Per-section scope.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · What the migration loses：Not lost: sealing. A preset fixes an agent's composition when the agent is created and is not retrofitted into a live one, so the "start a new session to apply it" behavior carries over unchanged.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Overview：`@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles` adds a second axis to a DeepSeek Harness profile. Agent presets decide what an agent is: which tools and behaviors are available. Prompt profiles decide how that agent is told to work. The same agent with the same tools can run as a terse reviewer or as a specialist that follows a house style, and the only thing that changes is the profile you pick at session start.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Overview：A profile is an ordered list of references to reusable sections. Every reference carries its own position and scope, so a single section can appear in several profiles in a different place each time. The profile is chosen when a session starts, sealed into that session's prompt, and never revised afterwards. Choose no profile and the system prompt is not modified at all.

The editor and the composer chip live in the web GUI, so you build profiles without hand-editing a single prompt string.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Features：- Reusable sections: write a fragment once, reference it from any number of profiles, each reference with its own order and scope.
- Per-reference scope (`inherit`, `main-only`, `subagents-only`): a subagent can receive guidance its parent session never sees, and the same section can be narrowed to one context in one profile while staying broad in another.
- Deterministic ordering: sections emit in profile order and take a stable position among the platform's built-in prompt material.
- Sealed sessions: the profile is resolved while the session prompt is assembled and fixed from then on, so resuming a session reproduces exactly what it started with.
- Explicit opt-out: picking None is a recorded decision rather than a missing value, and it seals the same way a profile does.
- Zero footprint by default: with no profile selected, prompt assembly is untouched.
- Composer chip: choose the profile for the next session next to the permission and plan chips, and the choice is remembered per workspace.
- Graceful skips: an unknown, out-of-scope, disabled, empty, or unresolvable section is left out of the prompt instead of breaking the session.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Install：```bash
dsh plugin --profile web add @knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles
```

From a local checkout or a git URL:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile web add /path/to/dsh-prompt-profiles
```

`lib/` ships prebuilt, so installing never runs a build. A first install can come up through hot module replacement, while replacing an installed copy needs a DSH restart.

Remove it with:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile web remove @knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles
```
@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Quick start：Sessions already running keep the prompt they were sealed with, so a profile applies to sessions you start from now on.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · The composer chip：- It renders only on a blank session and only when at least one profile exists.
- `None` opts a session out explicitly and seals that decision.
- The choice is remembered per workspace, so the next session in the same workspace starts with the same profile.
- In a complete mode (for example `minimal`, whose preset sets `config.complete: true`) the engine discards every prompt section. The chip marks the trigger with a warning and the profile has no effect there.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · The editor：**Settings → Prompt profiles** has three tabs: Profiles, Sections, and Preview.

The `Profiles` tab lists every profile with its section count and sets the default for new sessions.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · The editor：Opening a profile shows its sections in prompt order with the platform's built-in sections displayed in place among them, so you can see where your text lands in the assembled prompt. Drag the handle or type an order number to move a row, pick a scope on each row, and use the row icons to edit or remove a section. Duplicate and delete sit next to each profile in the list.

The `Sections` tab lists every section with the profiles that use it, and filters by id and title.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · The editor：A section carries a title and a body, and edits save automatically after a short pause. A section owned by another bundle keeps its id locked and can only be disabled. Renaming an id never rewrites profile references; the response names the profiles that still hold the old id so you can fix them by hand.

The `Preview` tab shows the selected profile in position among the built-in prompt sections and lists everything it skipped, with the reason for each skip.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Prompt variables：Section bodies may contain `{{name}}` references, for example `{{cwd}}`. The runtime substitutes them strictly when the session prompt is sealed: an unknown or malformed reference makes the sealer drop that section rather than emit a broken prompt. The editor preview is deliberately lenient, and it reports such a section as skipped with the reason, so you see what the runtime would discard instead of text it would never produce.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Where data lives：| Data | Location |
|---|---|
| Section and profile definitions, per-row overrides | the profile's patch rows in `cordis.patch.yml`, written by this bundle's writer |
| `default` and `lastByWorkspace` | volatile settings of the `prompt-profiles` main row |
| Sealed per-session snapshots | `$DSH_HOME/storages/prompt_profiles/sessions/<sessionId>.json`, one record per session |

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Requirements：- DSH in `>=0.1.7-rc.2 <0.2.2-0` — the peer window this bundle declares; `0.2.1-alpha.2` is the release it is verified on.
- Outside that window DSH disables the plugin until you grant it the exact-version exemption (`dsh plugin allow-version`).
- The installed profile's own plugins: on the host `settings`, `configEditor`, `workspaceRegistry`, `storageDomain`, `typert` and `agentPresets`; on the web client `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-settings`, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-conversation` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-primitives`.
- A missing optional service degrades one feature. It does not block the mount.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Develop：```bash
mise install          # Node, pnpm and the DSH release the bundle targets
pnpm install --store-dir ./.pnpm-store
pnpm run build        # esbuild bundles + tsc declarations into lib/
pnpm test             # host unit and differential tests (node --test)

`lib/` is build output and is committed on purpose: profile installs must not require a build. See [SPEC.md](SPEC.md) for the product contract and the module contracts under [src/](src/) for implementation responsibilities.

@knopki/dsh-prompt-profiles README · Known limitations：- One DSH process. Writes from a single DSH process are coordinated; a second DSH process editing the same profile patch can overwrite rows or choices.
- Strict sealing. A session's decision is made once and never revised, an empty decision included. A session that started before its snapshot record existed keeps its result, so start a new session to get a profile into it.
